additions.reason: Eating beyond one's need is the first pole of the Torah's central bechina. The Rebbe establishes this concept by stating: when a person eats more than they need, the food harms them. The reason: the food is left without a living recipient to receive vitality from. This state is then explicitly equated (bechina) with placing food into a vessel. Node does not exist in the dataset for Torah #257.
additions.source_quote: כְּשֶׁאוֹכֵל יוֹתֵר מִצָּרְכּוֹ, זֶה הַמַּאֲכָל מַזִּיק לוֹ

additions.reason: The vessel (כלי) is the bechina-equivalent of overeating. Food placed in a vessel receives no vitality because a vessel cannot serve as a living recipient. This is the explicit metaphor and the hermeneutic key to 'וְאֶל כֶּלְיְךָ לֹא תִתֵּן'. The keli is a neutral structural object — it describes the inert, non-receiving state. Node does not exist in the dataset for Torah #257.
additions.source_quote: וְהוּא דּוֹמֶה כְּאִלּוּ הִנִּיחוֹ הָאָדָם לְתוֹךְ כְּלִי, שֶׁבְּוַדַּאי אֵינוֹ מְקַבֵּל חִיּוּת מִשָּׁם

additions.reason: The Torah introduces the concept that every created thing has a 'root' (שרש) from which it receives its vitality (חיות). This root/vitality concept is the metaphysical premise of the entire teaching. However, the relationship between שרש and חיות in this Torah is more eitza than bechina — the root IS the source THAT GIVES vitality (cause-effect framing: 'יש לו שרש שיש לו חיות ממנו'). It is therefore borderline: one could argue שרש and חיות are two names for the same anchoring principle (bechina), but the text frames it causally. If added as bechina, these two would form a second small package or extend Package 1 as the positive pole (receiving vitality = being rooted) vs. the negative pole (keli = rootless). Flagged here as a candidate for review rather than a firm addition.
additions.source_quote: כִּי כָּל דָּבָר יֵשׁ לוֹ שֹׁרֶשׁ שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ חִיּוּת מִמֶּנּוּ

additions.reason: Eating exactly what one needs (צרכו / כנפשך שבעך) is the positive pole implied by the teaching — it is the state in which the food-person relationship is alive and mutual. The verse 'וְאָכַלְתָּ כְּנַפְשְׁךָ שָׂבְעֲךָ' defines the proper boundary. While not explicitly stated as a bechina node, צרכו is the structural counterpart to אכילה יתרה within the same domain — one is the living-root state, the other is the keli-state. If the dataset were to capture this Torah fully, צרכו would be either a node in Package 1 (the non-keli state) or an eitza concept (eating properly leads to receiving the food's vitality).
additions.source_quote: וְזֶה: וְאָכַלְתָּ כְּנַפְשְׁךָ שָׂבְעֲךָ – לֹא יוֹתֵר

analysis_notes.note_on_zero_dataset_edges: Torah #257 is entirely absent from torahData.js. All 2 proposed package nodes and 4 gap-analysis additions are sourced exclusively from the source text. This Torah needs to be fully entered into the dataset.
analysis_notes.note_on_good_evil_mirror: Torah #257 does not exhibit a classic good/evil polarity mirror structure. The teaching operates entirely in the neutral domain of physical causality (food, vitality, the body). There is no explicit evil force, no sitra achra, no yetzer hara. The only polarity present is 'correct amount vs. excess' — and both poles are neutral (they describe a physical state, not a spiritual alignment). Package 1 is therefore marked 'neutral'.
analysis_notes.note_on_story_frame: The opening narrative about the mother's testament (שהניחה לו אמו צוואה — that whoever cannot tolerate someone should not allow him near) is described as being explained 'elsewhere' (ויתבאר במקום אחר). It is explicitly bracketed off from the conceptual content of this Torah and should not be treated as bechina material here.
